agent-task-spec-first-try.title: How do you write a coding-agent task that succeeds on the first try?
agent-task-spec-first-try.summary: A good agent task has four parts: context, a definition of done, boundaries, and verification. It takes five minutes to write and saves most rework cycles.
agent-task-spec-first-try.hook: I run coding agents every day, and the biggest difference in output comes from five minutes of task writing, long before the model choice. In my PR Description post I covered how to explain a change to a human reviewer. This is the exact same work, one step earlier: the moment you write the task for the agent.
agent-task-spec-first-try.body:
**Short answer:** A good agent task has four parts: context, a definition of done, boundaries, and verification. It takes five minutes to write and saves most rework cycles.

### The context the agent can't guess

The agent sees the code, but not the reason it looks that way. One line on why the change is needed, and one more on what you already tried, saves most wrong directions. If one file holds the problem, point to it by name.

### A definition of done before you start

"Fix the form" is an open-ended task. "The form saves, shows an error on an empty field, and the existing tests pass" is a task you can check. An explicit definition of done turns your job from supervising every step into one check at the end.

### Boundaries in writing

An agent that finds a nearby problem tends to fix that too. Write what's in scope and what stays out: which folder it may touch, whether it may change an existing API, and whether it may upgrade a dependency. The boundary becomes part of the task, not a negotiation after the output.

### The check that proves the output works

Write how to verify: which command runs the tests, and what result to expect. The agent checks itself before handing back, and you look at evidence, not vibes.

### A full task in four lines

Example: "checkout.ts has a bug: double-clicking submit creates two orders. Done = double-click creates one order, all tests pass. Boundaries = only checkout.ts and its tests, no dependency upgrades. Verify = npm test checkout."

### How much time this saves

Five minutes of writing versus two or three fifteen-minute rework cycles. In my experience, most of those cycles start with a task missing one of the four parts.
faq: How long should an agent task be?
Long enough to cover the four parts. Usually five to ten lines. A task that's too long hides what matters, and a one-line task only fits a pinpoint change.
What do you do when the agent steps out of bounds?
Stop, sharpen the boundary in the task, and rerun from a clean state. Fixing the output by hand leaves the next task at the same level.
Do you need a full task for a small change too?
A one-line change in one file needs one line. The four parts come into play the moment the change touches more than one file or one decision.

agent-skill-vs-rules-file.title: When do repeated agent instructions become a Skill?
agent-skill-vs-rules-file.summary: A fact about the project belongs in the rules file. A process that repeats itself belongs in a Skill. The practical difference: the rules file always loads and costs in every conversation, and a Skill loads only when needed. Rule of thumb: if you've pasted the same instruction three times, it's time to give it a home.
agent-skill-vs-rules-file.hook: In my post I told how my bot started its own open source project and even published its failure in the README. After weeks of working this way I noticed I was pasting the same instructions to it again and again. The Claude Code documentation on Skills has a precise answer for when those instructions should become a file, and when they should become a Skill.
agent-skill-vs-rules-file.body:
**Short answer:** A fact about the project belongs in the rules file. A process that repeats itself belongs in a Skill. The practical difference: the rules file always loads and costs in every conversation, and a Skill loads only when needed. Rule of thumb: if you've pasted the same instruction three times, it's time to give it a home.

### A rules file is facts, a Skill is a process

The Claude Code docs draw the line explicitly: create a Skill when you keep pasting the same instructions, the same checklist, or the same multi-step process, or when part of the rules file grows into a process instead of a fact. "We work with TypeScript strict" is a fact. "This is how we open a PR, step by step" is a process.

Example: a rule saying "every PR includes a description of the decision" stays in the rules file. A six-step process for checking a migration before merging becomes a Skill.

### Why the fixed loading cost matters

Everything in the rules file loads into every conversation, even when it's irrelevant. A Skill loads only when the agent detects it's needed or when it's called by name. For a team, that means you can maintain a whole library of processes without inflating every conversation. The docs put it this way: the Skill body costs almost nothing until it's used.

### How to start in practice

First step: open your conversation history and look for an instruction you pasted twice or more. Second: write it once as a SKILL.md with a short name and a description of when to use it. Third: try it on a real task and fix the wording based on what the agent actually did, not what you wanted it to do.

In my work with the agent on its open source project, I learned that the name and description are what the agent reads to decide whether the Skill is relevant. A vague description means a Skill that never opens, or opens at exactly the wrong moment.

### Testing that the Skill works

After writing it, run the process on a real case and check three things: the agent opened the Skill on time, followed the steps in order, and the output matches what you would have done manually. If one of the three fails, fix the SKILL.md, not the output. Fixing the output hides the problem for next time.
faq: What's the difference between a Skill and a prompt saved in a file?
A Skill carries a name, a description of when to use it, and helper files, and the agent decides to load it when relevant. A saved prompt still requires you to remember to paste it.
How many Skills is normal to keep?
As many as you have real recurring processes. The risk isn't quantity but vague descriptions, which make the agent pick the wrong Skill.
And the rules file, still relevant?
Yes, for stable facts about the project: language, conventions, constraints. Anything that's a process with steps moves to a Skill.

agent-payment-approval-limits.title: How do you let an AI agent pay without losing control?
agent-payment-approval-limits.summary: The agent gets a dedicated payment rail with a cap, not an open card. Every unusual charge goes through human approval, and the log gets read once a week. The agent can order, compare prices, and close a purchase, but the amount it can get wrong is capped in advance.
agent-payment-approval-limits.hook: In my post about Hark I told about a company that handed out real pizzas worth a million dollars: you write to the agent in chat, and it orders from DoorDash on your card. My agent orders and pays for real things too. The question isn't whether to let it pay, but how to stay in control of every shekel.
agent-payment-approval-limits.body:
**Short answer:** The agent gets a dedicated payment rail with a cap, not an open card. Every unusual charge goes through human approval, and the log gets read once a week. The agent can order, compare prices, and close a purchase, but the amount it can get wrong is capped in advance.

### Separate approval from execution

My first rule: the agent prepares the order, a human approves the payment. It sounds cumbersome, and in practice it's ten seconds of approval in chat. What you gain is that there's no scenario where one morning you discover a charge nobody asked for.

Example: the agent sends "Found the cable for 89 shekels including shipping, approve?". The answer "yes" is the approval. No "yes", no charge.

### A monetary cap, not a feeling of safety

A solution that works is a dedicated card or a separate allowance with a small monthly cap. If the agent gets it wrong, the maximum damage is the cap. On our team the same principle applies to paid dev tools: every new integration starts with a limited budget, and expands only after a month of clean usage.

A number worth keeping in mind: a monthly cap of 500 shekels costs less than one hour of a team member's work, and it turns the agent's most expensive mistake into something you can sign off calmly.

### A log that actually gets read

Every charge the agent makes goes into one list: what was bought, how much, when, and which request stood behind it. Once a week, five minutes of reading. Just like I found out my meeting recordings had stopped only after a whole week, small charges can pile up unnoticed. The weekly digest catches that.

### What not to do

Don't give the agent the business's main card. Don't rely on "it promised to ask". And don't connect a payment method without checking how to cancel: before the first connection, verify you can freeze the card or close the allowance in one click.
faq: And how much time does it take a human to approve each time?
Ten seconds of approval in chat. That's the price of control, and it's cheap compared to a wrong charge you have to chase.
Can you give the agent a budget with no approval at all?
Yes, within a low cap you're willing to lose. Above the cap, human approval comes back.
What do you do if the agent already charged something wrong?
Freeze the payment method, contact the vendor for a refund, and update the rules so that case doesn't repeat. The log shows exactly which request led to the charge.

agent-talk-from-content-archive.title: How do you turn a year of personal writing into a talk with an agent?
agent-talk-from-content-archive.summary: Collect the raw material into one file, write a brief with audience, goal, and time, ask for an outline before slides, and check every claim against the source before approving a slide. The agent is excellent at synthesizing existing material, and the responsibility for accuracy stays with you.
agent-talk-from-content-archive.hook: In my post about the talk built from WhatsApp I told how I gave an agent a file with a year of my posts and asked for a talk on turning an entire company AI-native. I got a 15-slide deck and a prep guide, including the demo. Here is the process that worked, and what you must check before getting on stage with it.
agent-talk-from-content-archive.body:
**Short answer:** Collect the raw material into one file, write a brief with audience, goal, and time, ask for an outline before slides, and check every claim against the source before approving a slide. The agent is excellent at synthesizing existing material, and the responsibility for accuracy stays with you.

### Collect the material before asking for output

My agent got a file with a year of my LinkedIn posts. That's what allowed it to find a real line of thinking instead of a generic deck about AI. Without your own material, you'll get a talk anyone could give.

Example: one tidy file sorted by date, with a link to every source. Thirty full posts beat 200 summary lines.

### Write a brief of audience, goal, and time

"Prepare a talk for me" returns something generic. A brief that works answers three questions: who sits in the audience, what should they do differently after the talk, and how many minutes you have. Mine was small business owners, 45 minutes, and one goal: that they go home with a first task they can give an agent.

### Ask for an outline before slides

The cheapest time to fix a talk is before it's a deck. Ask for an outline first: an arc, a core message per part, and at least one demo. After the outline is approved, ask for slides and a prep guide.

A prep guide is worth no less than the slides: what to say on each slide, how much time per part, and where to stop for questions.

### Check every claim against the source

The agent phrases confidently even when it's half-accurate. Every number, date, or tool name on a slide needs backing: a link to the source in the raw material, or a current official document. An unsupported claim leaves the deck.

Example: if a slide says "companies adopting agents save 30% of development time" and there's no source, replace it with data you can show, or with a sentence about your own experience only. Anthropic's long-context prompting guidelines also recommend giving concrete examples and asking for a quote from the source before synthesis, which is exactly this check.

### Prepare a short emergency version

Half an hour before the conference, things break: the projector, the power, the network. Keep a ten-minute version: three points, one example, one message. If everything collapses, you still deliver value.
faq: How long does a process like this take?
The production itself is fast. Most of the time goes to checking against sources and rehearsing, and you can't shorten those without paying in quality.
Can the agent deliver the talk too?
You can't delegate the responsibility. It's your talk, your claims, and the audience asks you.
What if my posts aren't rich enough for a talk?
Start with the question the audience keeps asking you. A small archive with real experience is worth more than a big archive of generalities.

agent-long-creative-build-feedback.title: How do you run a long creative project with an AI agent through chat?
agent-long-creative-build-feedback.summary: Define a clear final output, grant access gradually by stage, agree on regular reporting with screenshots, fix one comment per round, and check the output in the real system. A short loop with verification works better than one big task with no stops.
agent-long-creative-build-feedback.hook: In my post about the Roblox game I told how Instinct built Royal Chair within days, through my WhatsApp: it reported, sent screenshots, and got comments and fixes from me. This guide breaks that working method into steps. It documents one case that worked, not a promise that every project ends this way.
agent-long-creative-build-feedback.body:
**Short answer:** Define a clear final output, grant access gradually by stage, agree on regular reporting with screenshots, fix one comment per round, and check the output in the real system. A short loop with verification works better than one big task with no stops.

### Start with a brief you can check

Before the agent touches a tool, write what the final output is and how you'll know it works. In my case the brief was a simple fighting game with chairs, short rules, and a name. The more measurable the result, the fewer rounds wasted on guessing.

Example: instead of "build me a fun game", write "a single-player fighting game, three weapons, a win after five minutes, a victory screen with the winner's name". Every line like that can be checked at the end.

### Grant access gradually, not all at once

A long project through chat means the agent works while you're not watching. Open only what the stage requires: environment installation at the start, write permission to one project, and publishing only after explicit approval. The Roblox Studio setup documentation separates installing the environment from opening a project, and that's the right working order even when an agent performs the steps.

If a stage requires a new account or a payment, that's your stop, not the agent's. Agree on this upfront, so the work doesn't get stuck on a payment screen in the middle of the night.

### Agree on regular reporting

The part that worked best for me: the agent reported to WhatsApp at fixed points, attached screenshots from the build, and waited for comments. Without regular reporting, a long project becomes a black box that arrives at the end with surprises.

Example: a report after every milestone, three lines - what was built, what actually came out versus the plan, and what the open question is. One screenshot is worth more than a paragraph of description.

### One comment per round

When a screenshot shows a problem, fix that alone. "The character is stuck in the wall" is a comment. "Improve the gameplay, change the lighting, and add a level" are three tasks that tangle together. Every round: a comment, a fix, a new screenshot proving the fix worked.

The wording of the comment matters too. "The chair doesn't look good" leaves the agent guessing. "The chair is half sunk in the floor, raise it to sitting height" is a comment that can be executed and checked.

### Check in the real system

A screenshot is evidence, not a test. At the end of every significant stage, enter the system yourself: run it, click, look for the scenarios from the brief. Only after that do you approve moving to the next stage.

Anything not checked in the real system doesn't count as closed, even if the agent reports "done".
faq: Can you let the agent work a whole night without reports?
You can, but every hour without a report is an hour where a wrong direction gets more expensive. A reporting point every hour or two keeps the risk small.
What do you do when the agent is stuck on the same problem?
Stop the round, ask it to phrase what it knows and what's missing, then decide: missing information, missing permission, or a wrong approach. Don't let it retry the same step again and again.
Does the method fit code too, not just games?
Yes. A checkable brief, gradual access, regular reporting, and one comment per round work the same way on a feature, a document, or a deck.

weekly-agent-digest.title: How do you build a weekly digest that turns agent output into visible work?
weekly-agent-digest.summary: Set a fixed format with three questions - what came in, what turned into work, what got stuck - and run the daily output through it once a week, at a fixed time. The digest is not another report. It's the decision point where output becomes action or gets dropped.
weekly-agent-digest.hook: In that same post I told how, after the recordings stopped for a week, I added a weekly digest: a fixed point where you see what came in, what turned into work, and what got stuck. Here is the full format and the rules that keep it useful.
weekly-agent-digest.body:
**Short answer:** Set a fixed format with three questions - what came in, what turned into work, what got stuck - and run the daily output through it once a week, at a fixed time. The digest is not another report. It's the decision point where output becomes action or gets dropped.

### The problem with daily output

An agent that works every day produces a pile: summaries, reminders, suggestions, links. Nobody reads a daily pile for long. What doesn't get used gets forgotten, and what gets forgotten gets missed. One week without review, and the output becomes background noise.

### The format: three questions, not a table of contents

What came in? The list of items the agent produced this week, unedited. The goal is coverage, not readability.

What turned into work? For every item that became an action - a task, a message sent, a decision - one line. This is the only metric that matters: output that turned into motion.

What got stuck? Items that came back week after week with no motion. A stuck item gets an explicit decision: push it forward, drop it, or change the way it arrives.

Example: one week brought fourteen items. Five turned into work: two messages sent, two drafts queued, and one document updated. Three items got stuck for a second consecutive week, and the decision was to take them off the daily list instead of dragging them along again.

### Rules that keep the digest useful

A fixed time. Same hour every week, regardless of load. A digest postponed twice is dead.

A decision criterion for every stuck item. If an item hasn't moved in two weeks, it leaves or changes. No third option of "we'll decide later".

A small number. If the list is too long for a ten-minute review, the problem is the daily output, not the digest. Shrink the source, not the review.

### What this gives you in practice

The digest turns the agent from an output machine into a work tool. Instead of remembering to check what happened, there's a fixed point where you see what came in, what turned into work, and what got stuck. The template I work with is in my public skills library, and you can install it as is.
faq: What's the difference between a digest and a daily summary?
A daily summary describes what happened. A weekly digest is a decision point: what turned into work, what got stuck, and what you decide about each stuck item.
How long should the weekly review take?
About ten minutes. If it needs more, the daily output is too noisy and worth shrinking at the source.
What do you do with an item stuck two weeks in a row?
Decide: push it now, drop it, or change the form it arrives in. No fourth option of quiet postponement.

monthly-automation-review.title: How do you check after a month that the automation really works?
monthly-automation-review.summary: Don't assume it ran. Open the actual output, compare it to what the automation was supposed to produce, and decide for each component: keep, change, or stop. Without comparing to real output, an automation can stop quietly and nobody notices.
monthly-automation-review.hook: In my post I told how my meeting recordings stopped for a whole week and I found out only by chance, when I asked the bot what it did with the material. Here I turn the monthly check I ran into a work list: what to check, how to decide, and when to stop.
monthly-automation-review.body:
**Short answer:** Don't assume it ran. Open the actual output, compare it to what the automation was supposed to produce, and decide for each component: keep, change, or stop. Without comparing to real output, an automation can stop quietly and nobody notices.

### Why automations stop quietly

Most automations don't alert when they stop. A third-party service changes a permission, a process crashed and nobody restarted it, or the output keeps being produced but never reaches its destination. From the outside everything looks fine, because nobody looks at the output itself.

In the post I published I told how my meeting recordings stopped for a whole week, and I found out only when I asked the bot what it did with the material. That's exactly the problem: the check started only when someone asked.

### An end-of-month checklist

For each automation, three questions in order:

What was it supposed to produce? A concrete output: a recording per meeting, a daily summary, an updated file. If you can't phrase the output in one sentence, the automation isn't defined well enough.

What was actually created? Open the latest output itself. Not the log, not the settings. The artifact you were supposed to use.

What's the decision? For each component, one of three: keep, change, or stop. An automation whose output nobody reads costs more than it gives.

Example: an automation meant to summarize ten meetings a week. The review finds summaries for only six. Check the missing four: two meetings were canceled, one wasn't recorded because of a permission, and one was recorded but never sent. The decision: fix the permission and add an existence check for the output, not replace the tool.

### When to change and when to stop

Change when the output arrives but isn't usable: an inconvenient format, too-high frequency, noise instead of signal. Stop when usage has disappeared even though the output is fine. A review that ends without a single stop is a sign the list wasn't really made, or the check was shallow.

My full list for a review like this - what to keep, what to change, and what to stop - also went into my public skills library, so it can be run again and again without rewriting.
faq: Why not settle for the automation's logs?
Because a log says the process ran, not that the output arrived and someone used it. The real check is opening the latest artifact itself.
How often should you check?
A full review once a month, and a short existence check of the output once a week. An automation critical to daily work needs a higher frequency.
What do you do with an automation whose output nobody reads?
Stop it. Output nobody consumes is cost without benefit, and sometimes an unnecessary privacy risk too.

golden-sample-agent-quality-cost-check.title: How do you check that a multi-agent process is worth its cost?
golden-sample-agent-quality-cost-check.summary: Build a small sample with known answers, run a single agent and a multi-agent process on it, and compare three metrics: how many of the right answers were found, how many errors were added, and what the cost was. Decide by the metrics, not by an impression from a demo.
golden-sample-agent-quality-cost-check.hook: In my post about Dynamic Workflows I mentioned an Anthropic demo on Latent Space: a multi-agent process that cost much more than a single agent and also found more. Before copying an approach like that to a real task, I build a sample of known answers and compare. Here is how the test is built.
golden-sample-agent-quality-cost-check.body:
**Short answer:** Build a small sample with known answers, run a single agent and a multi-agent process on it, and compare three metrics: how many of the right answers were found, how many errors were added, and what the cost was. Decide by the metrics, not by an impression from a demo.

### Build a sample with known answers

Pick 10 to 30 items from the real material. For some items the right answer is known in advance: for example a document that contains a specific commitment, or a clean document with no finding at all. Write the answers down before any run.

Example: when testing 200 documents against a new policy, pick 20 documents, manually mark which commitments appear in them, and keep the list as an answer key.

### Run two setups on the same sample

One run with a single agent handling all items. A second run with a multi-agent process, for example reader agents, checker agents, and a report-joining step. Same items, same instruction, same model version.

### Measure three numbers

Accuracy: how many of the findings from the key were found in each run. Noise: how many wrong findings were added. Cost: tokens, run time, and how many repeat passes were needed.

In the Anthropic demo on Latent Space, a stock-list scan with a review stage cost much more than a single agent and also found more details in the example. That's the illustration of the tradeoff between cost and coverage. Your sample is what tells you whether the tradeoff pays off on your task.

### Decide by the result

If the multi-agent process found more correct findings at a cost you're willing to pay, expand gradually. If a single agent reached the same result, stay with it. For a small set of independent parts, even a simple script can be the answer.

### What to keep from the test

Keep the answer key, both reports, and the comparison table. When someone later asks why you chose one architecture over another, you have numbers from your task, not a quote from somebody else's demo.
faq: How big should a test sample be?
10 to 30 real items with known answers are enough for a first comparison. The goal is a signal on quality and cost, not statistical proof.
What if a single agent and a multi-agent process reached the same result?
Stay with the single agent. It's simpler to run, maintain, and explain. Expand only when the sample shows a measurable gain.
How do you measure the cost of an agent run?
Record tokens, run time, and the number of repeat passes for each run on the same sample, and compare against the accuracy gain you got.

agent-workflow-guardrails-before-scaling.title: Which boundaries do you set before running dozens of AI agents in parallel?
agent-workflow-guardrails-before-scaling.summary: Four boundaries: a session budget, minimal permissions, a full coverage list, and output checked against a criterion. Write them before the first run, test on a small sample, and only then increase parallelism.
agent-workflow-guardrails-before-scaling.hook: In my post about Dynamic Workflows I described Anthropic's new beta for agent orchestration inside Claude Managed Agents, and ended with four things worth defining before trying it. Here I turn those four into an ordered work list, with the reasoning from the documentation and the way I check things like this on a team.
agent-workflow-guardrails-before-scaling.body:
**Short answer:** Four boundaries: a session budget, minimal permissions, a full coverage list, and output checked against a criterion. Write them before the first run, test on a small sample, and only then increase parallelism.

### Budget: set at session opening

In Claude Managed Agents you set the budget when creating the session. You can't add a budget to a session that's already running. When the session reaches the budget, runs are paused. Requests that already started can complete and exceed the budget. A run paused over budget resumes when you raise or remove it.

Example: in a session checking 200 documents against a new policy, set a budget that covers one full pass plus a little for repeat checks. If the run stops midway, you know the initial estimate was too low.

### Permissions: start read-only

The ability to split work among agents is no reason to give every agent permission to change data or send messages. Every thread inside the session has its own event stream, and tool permissions can be managed per thread.

A good opening check: reader agents return findings only. Only one stage, if any, gets write permission, and it's limited to a single destination.

### Coverage: a closed list of items

Define upfront the list of items the run should handle. Every item ends in one of two states: checked, or not checked with a reason. A report that looks complete without a coverage list is not evidence.

The Dynamic Workflows documentation lists system limits: up to 64 threads in parallel per run, and up to 1,000 agents over a run's lifetime. Those are technical ceilings. A useful starting point is on the order of dozens of items and a few agents.

### Verification: completed is not a sign the work succeeded

The documentation states explicitly: a completed status means the plan finished. It doesn't mean all the work succeeded. Check the output itself against a criterion defined upfront: how many items were covered, how many findings verified, how many rejected and why.

### A suggested working order

1. Write the four boundaries into the task itself, before the run.
2. Run on a small sample with known answers.
3. Compare output, coverage, and cost against a single agent.
4. Increase parallelism only after the metrics show a real gain.
faq: Why set the budget at session opening?
Because in Claude Managed Agents you can't add a budget to an existing session. When the budget is reached, runs are paused, and requests that already started can complete and exceed it.
Is a completed status enough to trust the output?
No. Completed means the plan finished. Check the output against a criterion: coverage, verified findings, and reasons for rejections.
How many agents make sense in a first test?
A few agents over dozens of items. The documentation allows up to 64 parallel threads and up to 1,000 agents over a run, and those are ceilings, not a starting point.

agent-onboarding-completed-task-metrics.title: How do you measure the start of AI agent usage beyond signup?
agent-onboarding-completed-task-metrics.summary: Define separate stages for joining, connecting, task attempt, a checked result, and repeat use. Measure each stage over the same period and the same user group, and mark where progress stopped. A signup is not proof of a completed task.
agent-onboarding-completed-task-metrics.hook: My post about the onboarding program separates people who joined through a link from participants in the program. That raises a different question from technical connection: which stage has already happened, and when can you say useful usage has begun? The numbers in the post and the image are historical documentation, not a new measurement in this guide.
agent-onboarding-completed-task-metrics.body:
**Short answer:** Define separate stages for joining, connecting, task attempt, a checked result, and repeat use. Measure each stage over the same period and the same user group, and mark where progress stopped. A signup is not proof of a completed task.

### Start with a definition of useful usage

Before a metrics table, pick one task the user wants to complete. Write down what output will be produced and what will be checked in it. A suggested example: the user asked for a comparison, received a document with sources, and checked that every threshold condition appears in it. The act of sending the message to the agent is an earlier stage.

Task completion should fit the type of work. Downloading a file doesn't prove its content is right. Connecting an account doesn't prove the agent performed a permitted action. If human approval is needed, define upfront whether "completed" includes the approval or stops at the draft.

### Separate events from interpretation

Build a clear stage list. A synthetic illustration for an onboarding flow: joined, completed a permitted connection, chose a task, received an output, checked a result, and returned for another task. Every stage needs an entry condition you can see, not a feeling from whoever is guiding.

In the Google Analytics documentation, an event measures an interaction on a site or app, and you can define a custom event when no existing event fits. That helps plan collection, but the event name is not business proof. An event called task_completed must be sent only when the agreed definition actually holds.

This guide does not recommend installing Analytics in every system. You can also start with minimal consented manual logging, without copying the task content or the conversation.

### Keep a base group and a measurement period

The total number of joiners and the number of this week's finishers are not the denominator and numerator of one measurement. The finishers may have joined earlier, or new joiners haven't had time to perform a task yet.

Choose a cohort of joiners and a follow-up window. A suggested example: everyone who joined in a given week, and whether they reached a checked output within the following seven days. This is an experiment proposal, not a window that fits every product. A task of a few hours and a task dependent on an external vendor need different time frames.

Also note in the report when the data was measured. An old snapshot doesn't become a fresh data point because the post was published again or later. The data date and the publication date should stay distinct.

### Look for the stopping point

A funnel report can show where people move between stages and where they drop. The Google Analytics documentation distinguishes between an open funnel, which allows entry at different stages, and a closed funnel that starts at the first stage. The choice changes who gets counted.

Even without an analytics tool, ask whether a person stopped because of connection, not choosing a task, an unclear output, or waiting for approval. Those are different problems. Sending everyone another reminder message doesn't automatically fix any of them.

The number of events is not the number of people. A repeated attempt can create several events for the same task. Define how you identify an attempt, how you handle duplicates, and what you count when a task is reopened.

### Add a small quality check

Check a sample of outputs against the agreed criteria, with permission to use the data. You can ask the user to mark what helped and what needed fixing without sending a whole private document.

Example: if ten documents were produced and sources were checked in only some of them, don't merge them into one line called "ten successes". You can report separately output that was returned and output that was checked. When there's no evidence of quality, write what's missing instead of completing the number to match expectation.

### End with one change you can test

Pick the prominent blocker and suggest a small change: clearer connection instructions, a shorter first task, or a result check that's easy to understand. Compare the same success definition in the next period, and note what changed.

Measurement should help people reach a result, not collect more information about them. Keep only what the question you defined requires, with proper consent and a clear retention period. A successful onboarding flow is useful usage you can explain, not growth in a number on a card.
faq: Does a signup count as agent usage?
It's a stage in the flow. To measure useful usage you need to define a task, an output, and a result check separately.
How do you compare weeks?
With the same base group, time window, and success definition. Document process changes so you don't attribute every difference to the tool itself.
Do you need to keep all conversations for measurement?
You can measure stages and limited feedback without keeping the content. The scope of collection and access requires consent and privacy planning.

mcp-first-read-connection-check.title: How do you verify an agent's MCP connection works, through the first read?
mcp-first-read-connection-check.summary: Check the connection in layers: address and transport, initialization and protocol version, tool discovery, and one permitted read. Record the result and the source, and separate a working connection from permission to perform further actions.
mcp-first-read-connection-check.hook: In my post about agent onboarding I also described tracking the first connection. When you connect an information source through MCP, the same question gets a technical test: did the client manage to read the right information, not just save an address in the settings? Here I propose a check sequence for such a connection, without claiming every participant connection in the program used MCP.
mcp-first-read-connection-check.body:
**Short answer:** Check the connection in layers: address and transport, initialization and protocol version, tool discovery, and one permitted read. Record the result and the source, and separate a working connection from permission to perform further actions.

### Define what the connection should return

An address saved in the settings is a start. A completion check should describe which information you can get and what should appear in the response. Pick a public item or a test datum with no private information. Write down the item's identifier, language, and expected source.

Example: when connecting to an instruction library, you want to fetch a specific instruction by identifier and compare the text to the published source. That check proves one read. It does not prove the agent can execute every instruction in the library or that it has access to accounts mentioned there.

### Check transport without inferring from the browser

An MCP server can run over a transport that isn't an HTML page. Opening the address in a browser and seeing an empty screen is not a protocol check. Even a healthy health response only checks what the server defined for that path.

Check the transport type both client and server support, the exact address, and the authentication requirements. Match the configuration to the client's documentation. A permission or Origin error is a finding to understand, not a reason to remove protections so the screen looks green.

### Complete the initialization step

In the MCP specification, the client starts with initialize, sends the protocol version and the capabilities it supports, and receives the server's version and capabilities. After success it sends notifications/initialized before normal activity.

Record which version was agreed. If the server returns a version the client doesn't support, per the spec the client should disconnect. Over an HTTP connection, follow-up requests should include the protocol version header per the spec. Better to use an MCP client that handles the lifecycle than to assume every single HTTP request is equivalent to a healthy connection.

### Discover a tool and understand its contract

A tools/list request returns the tools the server exposes. Read the name, description, and input schema. Ask whether the tool only reads information or changes external state. Match the first-read check to a tool whose effect is understood and permitted.

A readOnlyHint marker is a useful hint, but the spec says not to trust annotations from an untrusted source. Such a marker doesn't grant account access and doesn't replace testing the server. A new server declaring itself safe still requires verification of source and scope.

### Run one read and compare to the source

Pick a small input you're allowed to send. Check that the response contains the right item, not just valid JSON. If there's a public source, compare identifier, content, and language. If the result is marked stale, report that alongside the data. A cached response can be valid per the contract, but isn't necessarily current external state.

Alongside the success case, check a missing-identifier or invalid-input case. The goal is to know the client shows an understandable error and doesn't invent an answer in the tool's place. The test examples here are suggestions, not a report on a specific system that was tested.

### Hand over a state you can continue from

A short connection report can include: client and version, address and transport, agreed version, the tool checked, non-secret input, the read result, and what hasn't been verified yet. Avoid copying tokens, authentication headers, or a full conversation into the report.

That way you can say precisely "the connection returned this item". Expanding scope to more tools, writing, or private information is a separate test with separate permission. A first read is a starting point you can rely on, without turning it into a promise about every future task.
faq: Does a healthy health check prove the connection works?
It only proves the health check the server implemented. An MCP connection also requires initialization, tool discovery, and a read that matches the contract.
Is a tool marked read-only always safe?
It's a behavioral hint, not a permission or a proof of trustworthiness. Check source, input scope, and actual behavior.
What should you keep from the first-read report?
Versions, the tool, non-secret input, result, and limitations. Don't keep tokens or a full conversation just to prove connection.

browser-extension-race-condition-tests.title: How do you test race conditions in a browser extension an AI agent is changing?
browser-extension-race-condition-tests.summary: Define what must stay true when operations overlap, control their completion order in the test, and add a real-browser scenario. A test where two calls run one after the other doesn't prove the code handles overlap.
browser-extension-race-condition-tests.hook: In my post about the real-browser-mcp contribution I told about a contributor who came back after review with two separate PRs and fixes for cases that came up in testing. This guide proposes a working method you can apply to another contribution, without assuming every change has already been tested.
browser-extension-race-condition-tests.body:
**Short answer:** Define what must stay true when operations overlap, control their completion order in the test, and add a real-browser scenario. A test where two calls run one after the other doesn't prove the code handles overlap.

### Define the guarantee before writing the test

A browser extension connects local code to state that changes outside it. A tab can close, a group can change, and a debugging connection can end. So you need to ask what must hold between the start of an operation and its end.

In the public contribution to real-browser-mcp there was a case where two requests for a group name on the same tab could create two groups. PR number 71 describes a fix that serializes operations per tab and re-reads the tab state inside the lock. That's a concrete example of the same gap: the state read before the wait may be stale when the operation starts.

### Create overlap you can repeat

A synthetic illustration: two requests see a tab with no group. Each prepares to create a group. In a test you can hold the first call's promise open, start the second, and only then let the first complete.

At the end, check how many times group creation ran and what the tab's final state is. If the requirement is one group, two "success" results aren't enough. Ask the agent to show that under the same operation order the old version fails and the new one meets the requirement.

The example is a suggested way to test. The completion order should represent the real interface, not a substitute that only allows the order convenient for the code.

### Lock on the right resource

A per-tab lock can fit operations on the tab's group. A resource shared by the whole extension needs different thinking. PR number 72 describes a single queue for acquiring and using a debugger connection, to prevent two overlapping acquisitions with partial tracking.

The choice isn't "add a mutex" across the board. Define which operations share state, what can run in parallel, and when the protection is released. Also test an error inside the operation: a failure should leave a way for the next operation to proceed per the contract, not jam the queue.

### Separate an external signal from connection ownership

According to Chrome's documentation, a debugger connection that fails rejects the promise. An onDetach event arrives when the browser ends the session, for example when the tab closes or when DevTools opens on the connected tab.

A message about another debugger is not proof your extension holds the connection. PR number 72 describes a probe that tries to distinguish a connection the extension still holds after worker initialization from a connection failure. Both paths should be checked against the behavior the code actually implements.

### Add a test at the Chrome boundary

A unit test with a mock can control overlap and count calls. It doesn't prove that permissions, browser messages, and close events behave as you expected.

As suggested scenarios, check two overlapping requests, a tab closing mid-operation, and DevTools opening during a session. An extension using the debugger needs the debugger permission in the manifest. Using the tabGroups API requires the tabGroups permission. Match the permissions to the actual implementation, and don't add a permission just to make a test pass.

### Ask for a report that separates layers

At the end, the agent should state what was tested with a mock, what was tested in a browser, what the event order was, and on which version the test ran. There's no need to promise coverage of every possible race. There is a need for evidence of the discovered scenario and clear boundaries for what still needs testing.
faq: Is Promise.all enough to test a race?
It can start overlapping calls, but it doesn't guarantee the problematic order actually happened. Better to control the wait points and check the final state.
Should you lock every operation in the extension?
Choose protection by the shared state and the requirement. Too-wide a lock can prevent permitted parallelism; too narrow can leave a collision.
Does a mock test replace a browser test?
It helps control event order. Permissions, disconnections, and Chrome behavior also require a test at the real boundary.

review-feedback-to-verifiable-fix.title: How do you write review comments a coding agent or contributor can turn into a verified fix?
review-feedback-to-verifiable-fix.summary: Describe the problematic behavior, the conditions where it appears, and the result you want to keep. Ask for a focused fix and a test that fails against the old behavior. Separate a merge-blocking problem from an improvement suggestion that can wait.
review-feedback-to-verifiable-fix.hook: In my post about the real-browser-mcp contribution I told about a contributor who came back after review with two separate PRs and fixes for cases that came up in testing. This guide proposes a working method you can apply to another contribution, without assuming every change has already been tested.
review-feedback-to-verifiable-fix.body:
**Short answer:** Describe the problematic behavior, the conditions where it appears, and the result you want to keep. Ask for a focused fix and a test that fails against the old behavior. Separate a merge-blocking problem from an improvement suggestion that can wait.

### Start from a scenario, not a preference

A comment like "this needs tidying" leaves the real work with whoever received it. To turn a comment into a task, write what you can do in the system and what happens as a result.

In the public discussion on PR number 60 in real-browser-mcp, concrete problems appear: two operations in parallel on the same tab can create two groups, and two debugger connections can leave more than one tab attached when only one is tracked. The reply in the PR also describes what should be tested. These are sources for a scenario, not proof that every possible browser environment was tested.

### Write a short contract for the fix

The following wording is a suggested template:

> When two requests reach the same resource before the first finishes, the system should preserve the agreed result. Show a test that reproduces the collision against the old version, fix the behavior, and show the same test against the new version. State what wasn't tested.

"The agreed result" needs to be replaced with a real requirement: one group, one connection, or a clear error message. Each of these is a different decision. If there's no agreement, open a discussion before asking the agent to choose.

### Separate a blocker from a suggestion

A review can address a bug, a design question, and code cleanliness. Mark which kind of comment was written. A variable-name suggestion isn't equivalent to a permission fix, even if both appear in the same discussion.

The GitHub documentation describes three review states: comment, approve, and request changes. The ability of a request-changes to block a merge depends on the branch protection rules. Merely writing the word "blocker" in a comment isn't a technical rule definition in the repository.

### Keep the discussion small enough to verify

When a change includes two separate mechanisms, you can ask for a split. In the public example, tab-group management and debugger handling were separated into two PRs. The split lets you check intent and evidence for each part without tying them into one package of changes.

Splitting is a working tool, not a goal in itself. If two parts must land together to keep behavior correct, document the dependency and the merge order. An agent can prepare the branches, but the decision about the shared contract stays with the change owner.

### Check what changed after the comment

Before approving, read the new diff and the added test. Make sure the test touches the behavior raised in the discussion, not just the way the current code is written. Ask for a run result, a version, and a command. A planned test list in a PR body is not a run result.

If the agent summarizes "all comments handled", return it to the original list. Every comment needs a fix, an explanation of why it isn't required, or a decision to defer it. A conversation that scrolled off the screen is not evidence the problem is solved.

### Finish with a decision you can reconstruct

A good fix connects the comment, the requirement, and the evidence. That way, whoever reads the PR later can understand why the change went in and what it's supposed to preserve. The goal of a review is to improve the behavior and give a way to check it, without turning the person receiving the comment into a guesser.
faq: What's the difference between a comment and a request for changes?
GitHub supports comment, approve, and request changes as review states. Actual blocking depends on the branch rules, not only on the comment's wording.
Can an agent handle all review comments?
It can prepare fixes and evidence within agreed boundaries. A design question or a contract change requires an explicit decision.
When should you split a PR?
When there are separate mechanisms you can test separately. When there's a dependency, document it and the order the changes land.

agent-merge-conflict-intent.title: How do you let a coding agent resolve merge conflicts without losing the change's intent?
agent-merge-conflict-intent.summary: Hand the agent the goal of both changes, keep a return point, and check the combined result. Resolving a conflict isn't just removing markers from the file. You need to verify that the behavior each side meant to preserve still exists.
agent-merge-conflict-intent.hook: In my post about responsibility for a change I wrote that on the team we already built automations for opening PRs, self review, conflict fixing, and working on review comments. My emphasis moved to explaining the problem, the decision, and the risks. This guide proposes a way to turn that emphasis into a repeatable process.
agent-merge-conflict-intent.body:
**Short answer:** Hand the agent the goal of both changes, keep a return point, and check the combined result. Resolving a conflict isn't just removing markers from the file. You need to verify that the behavior each side meant to preserve still exists.

### Identify what's really colliding

A conflict says Git couldn't join part of the changes automatically. It doesn't decide which behavior is right. Both sides can be correct separately and still demand a new decision when joined.

Example: one branch adds a permission check before saving. Another branch changes the save to prevent a duplicate action. Choosing one side's version can erase the other's protection even if the code compiles. This is a synthetic example, not a fault recorded at a client.

### Keep a state you can explain and reconstruct

Before starting, check which branch you're on, which files changed, and what hasn't been saved yet. The Git documentation warns against merging with significant unsaved local changes. The git merge --abort command tries to restore the state before the merge, but doesn't guarantee restoring such local changes in every situation.

Ask the agent to identify the state and report it before acting. Don't let it delete local work to "clean" the working environment. A local commit or another form of saving should preserve the material, per the team's procedure. Secrets are not material you put in a commit.

### Give two intents, not just two files

Attach the reason for the change on each side, links to the discussion or PR description, and the tests that represent the behavior. Read the nearby code with the agent too. A variable-name change can hide a change in a function's contract.

A suggested request to the agent:

> Explain each side's intent and the collision. Propose a result that preserves both sides' requirements. If they contradict, stop with a focused question. Fix only the agreed conflict. Show a diff of the resolution and actual test results. Don't push or merge remotely without a separate instruction.

This defines an important boundary: the agent can prepare a local fix, but a product decision or a new permission requires whoever holds it to rule.

### Beware of automatic side-picking

In the Git documentation, the ours option inside a merge strategy prefers the current side in conflicting parts. The theirs option prefers the other side. These are technical rulings that can lose a requirement.

There's also a merge strategy called ours, which ignores the other side's changes and keeps the current side's tree. It's different from the option that prefers only conflicting parts. So a command that looks like a shortcut can change the meaning of the whole merge.

As a working default, ask for an explanation before a blanket choice. If the team decided to give up a change, document what was decided and why, instead of hiding the concession behind a "resolved" marker.

### Check the combination, not just the markers

The git diff --check command warns about conflict markers or whitespace errors added in the change. Per the Git documentation it returns a non-zero exit code when problems are found. It doesn't check that a permission, duplicate prevention, or other behavior was preserved.

Check a scenario representing each side, then a scenario exercising both together. In the permission-and-save example, check an authorized user, an unauthorized user, and a repeated action. The list is an illustration and depends on the code's real contract.

Alongside automated tests, go over the diff against the documented intents. Disappeared conflict markers are a stage in the process, not evidence of success.

### Return a short report before continuing

At the end the agent should present which conflicts were handled, what was preserved from each side, which commands ran, and what wasn't tested. An additional change needed to complete the join should be visible on its own.

If the result doesn't preserve both requirements, go back to the decision. The agent's role is to take down the mechanical work, without turning a business or engineering choice into something that happens by accident inside a file.
faq: Does no conflict markers mean the merge is right?
It means the markers were removed. You still need to check both sides' behavior and the combined result.
Does merge --abort always restore everything?
Git tries to reconstruct the state before the merge. When there's unsaved local work, restoration isn't guaranteed in every situation.
Does git diff --check check the logic?
It detects conflict markers and whitespace errors. Checking the behavior requires separate scenarios and evidence.

decision-first-pr-description.title: How do you write a PR description for code an AI agent wrote?
decision-first-pr-description.summary: Start with the problem and the decision, then describe the change, the risks, and the test evidence. Give the reviewer a way to understand why the change should land before they read the diff. The agent can prepare the draft, and the change owner checks it describes what actually happened.
decision-first-pr-description.hook: In my post about responsibility for a change I wrote that on the team we already built automations for opening PRs, self review, conflict fixing, and working on review comments. My emphasis moved to explaining the problem, the decision, and the risks. This guide proposes a way to turn that emphasis into a repeatable process.
decision-first-pr-description.body:
**Short answer:** Start with the problem and the decision, then describe the change, the risks, and the test evidence. Give the reviewer a way to understand why the change should land before they read the diff. The agent can prepare the draft, and the change owner checks it describes what actually happened.

### Write an explanation, not a file list

A list like "updated three files and added tests" helps orientation, but leaves the decision out of the picture. What was the problematic behavior? Why does this solution fit? What changed for whoever uses the system?

In a good PR description you can separate two things: the decision you can discuss and the code that implements it. If the decision is still open, say so. A description confident in itself doesn't turn an assumption into agreement.

### A template you can start from

The following text is a suggested template, not a description of a real PR:

> The problem: what can't the user or the system do today?
>
> The decision: which solution was chosen, and why? Which alternative was considered and what was the tradeoff?
>
> The change: what is the new behavior, and which components are affected?
>
> Boundaries: what stayed as it was, and what is explicitly outside the change?
>
> Evidence: which tests or scenarios actually ran, on which version, and what was the result?
>
> Risks: what might break, how will we detect it, and how can we roll back?
>
> Open questions: which decisions or checks are still missing?

The template should fit the change. A small fix doesn't need a long document. A change to permissions, data, or an external interface justifies extra explanation even if the diff is short.

### Ask the agent for evidence you can check

The agent can read the diff and the run results and propose a draft. Ask it to distinguish between "I ran" and "recommended to run". Every line about a test should rest on output or a result you can locate, not on a list of tests it intended to run.

Example: a change in invoice handling should describe what happens to an invoice that was paid while the work was queued. Unit test output helps, but doesn't by itself prove the payment-provider connection was checked. This is a suggested example, not a client case.

If the agent used test data or a service substitute, note that. If an integration test didn't run, leave the limitation visible instead of writing "everything works".

### Keep the responsibility with the change owner

Before opening the PR, read the description without the diff. Can you explain the decision in your own words? Is there a claim you didn't check? Is there a risk left that someone else needs to decide on?

The agent is a draft writer. Whoever brings the change to the team needs to hold the explanation. If you can't answer why a certain solution was chosen, go back to the decision conversation instead of adding more words to the description.

### Make the template part of the repository

Per GitHub's documentation, a PR template in the repository is shown automatically in the PR body when it's opened. You can keep it in a .github/pull_request_template.md file. To be available, the template needs to be merged into the default branch. Multiple templates are also supported, when change types call for different questions.

The template reminds you what to explain. It doesn't prove the explanation is right and doesn't replace testing or review. Every so often, check which fields repeat without adding information and which important questions stay outside it.

### Start with one decision you can review

Success here is that whoever does the review can identify the problem, understand the choice, and find test evidence, without guessing from file names. If the important question comes up only after reading hundreds of lines, move it forward into the description or into a discussion before the implementation.
faq: Can the agent write the PR description?

regression-first-agent-bugfix.title: How do you ask a coding agent to fix a bug with a regression test?
regression-first-agent-bugfix.summary: Keep a way to reproduce the failure before the change, define the wanted behavior, and ask for a small fix. The same test should catch the fault in the old code and pass on the fixed code, alongside tests for error scenarios.
regression-first-agent-bugfix.hook: In my post about moving from ask agent → hope to a working process I presented bug diagnosis as a sequence: reproduce, narrow down, hypothesis, measurement, and fix. Here I focus on the evidence that remains after the fix: a test that catches the old failure.
regression-first-agent-bugfix.body:
**Short answer:** Keep a way to reproduce the failure before the change, define the wanted behavior, and ask for a small fix. The same test should catch the fault in the old code and pass on the fixed code, alongside tests for error scenarios.

### Start from a reproducible failure

A description like "the screen sometimes breaks" leaves the agent too many options. Attach the input, the action performed, the expected result, and the actual result. Note version and environment when they affect the behavior. Remove private information from the example.

If the failure depends on timing or an external service, document what's known and what's still a hypothesis. Difficulty reproducing is important information, not a reason to present a fix as if the fault were already understood.

### Preserve the failure before touching the code

Ask the agent to add a focused test or a reproduction command and run it on the old version. Keep the output and the code version. A test written only after the fix can end up testing what the agent implemented instead of what the user needs.

Example: a function should read a settings file, but new exception handling returns an empty dictionary even when the file is missing. The regression test should demand the agreed error behavior, not settle for the function returning a dictionary. This is a suggested example, not a description of a client fault.

### Separate the environment from the behavior

In the pytest documentation, the fixture called tmp_path gives a separate temporary folder per test. You can create a valid file, a corrupt file, and a path that doesn't exist in it, without using personal files or the regular working directory.

The monkeypatch tool lets you temporarily change environment variables, attributes, or a function's behavior. The changes are undone when the test or fixture ends. It's useful for isolating an external dependency, but the result still depends on the substitute representing the interface correctly.

A test with a service substitute is not a connection test to the real service. State separately what was verified locally and what still needs an integration test. For temporary folders, use the safe defaults. An option like basetemp deletes the contents of the folder set for it, so it doesn't fit a path holding material you want to keep.

### Give the agent boundaries for the fix

You can use this request as an illustration:

> First reproduce the fault and keep a test that fails for the right reason. Explain the hypothesis and propose a small fix. Preserve the interface and the agreed error behavior. At the end show the diff, the commands, and the actual results, and what hasn't been tested yet. Any additional change beyond the fix requires a separate decision.

The boundaries prevent an overly broad solution: replacing a library, changing an output format, or hiding an exception can make the test pass without solving the original need.

### Check that the test really distinguishes the versions

Make sure the test fails on the old code because of the fault, not because of a missing dependency or an installation error. Then run it on the fix. If possible, temporarily check the test against the old version too, to confirm it still catches the failure.

Also run tests adjacent to the changed interface. A fix for file reading should address valid input, a missing file, and corrupt input per the function's contract. The list depends on the fault, and is no substitute for understanding the code.

### Return a result with evidence boundaries

At the end, keep the code version, the run commands, the result, and the limitations. Write "these tests passed" instead of "everything works". A change covering a local fault can still leave questions about another environment, large data, or an external service.

The role of a regression test is to leave evidence you can run after the conversation with the agent. It helps keep the fix as the code keeps changing.
faq: Is it enough that the agent wrote a passing test?
You need to verify the test catches the fault on the old version and passes on the fix. Green output alone doesn't prove that.
How do you test files without touching private data?
You can create synthetic inputs in a separate folder per test using tmp_path. Pick examples that represent the interface.
Does a mock replace an integration test?
It isolates a dependency and allows a focused test. The connection to the real service remains a separate test, and you should state if it wasn't done.

agent-wait-resume-without-duplicates.title: How do you give an AI agent a task that waits for a reply without creating duplicates?
agent-wait-resume-without-duplicates.summary: Define exactly what you're waiting to receive, when to stop waiting, and what needs re-checking before the action. Keep state and an identifier for the task, and verify the action is still needed when the reply arrives.
agent-wait-resume-without-duplicates.hook: In my post about waiting in a thread I described a request to Grok Bot to wait for a reply, then handle it if a ticket was sufficient. When the reply came, it found an existing ticket and returned it instead of opening a duplicate. This guide translates that case into a decision list you can check in another process.
agent-wait-resume-without-duplicates.body:
**Short answer:** Define exactly what you're waiting to receive, when to stop waiting, and what needs re-checking before the action. Keep state and an identifier for the task, and verify the action is still needed when the reply arrives.

### Turn waiting into part of the task

A task like "wait for a reply and then open a ticket" includes two different decisions. The first is identifying a relevant reply. The second is deciding whether a ticket is still needed. Between the request and the reply, a lot can change: someone else already handled it, a constraint was added, or the reply refers to a different request.

Write what the source is, which conversation or task it belongs to, and which reply allows continuing. A reply like "yes" without the context isn't a sufficient condition. Also keep the boundaries of the permitted action, instead of re-interpreting the consent hours later.

### Keep state you can return to

A short work record can hold a task identifier, the original request, the awaited source, the continuation condition, and the last verified state. Worth separating "waiting", "reply received", "current state checked", and "action completed".

Example: a request to collect a reply about a fault can stay in waiting state. After a reply that a ticket is sufficient, the agent checks whether a matching ticket exists. Only after creating or using an existing ticket and verifying the link can the task be marked completed. The example describes process design, not the outcome of a specific system.

The identifier should stay fixed even when an event is delivered twice. That way you can recognize a repeated delivery of the same reply instead of starting a new task.

### Re-check before acting

Before creating or updating, go back to the system where the action happens. Check whether the result already exists, who handled it, and whether the request is still valid. Memory of the state from before the wait is no substitute for this check.

If an earlier attempt ended without a clear response from the server, look for the result first. A timeout is not proof the action failed. Retrying without checking can create a duplicate precisely when the first action succeeded.

### Set an end to the wait

Write when the wait ends and what happens then: report to the task owner, close without action, or ask for a decision. A no-reply message should distinguish a source that didn't return a reply from a source that wasn't reachable.

When implementing part of the process in GitHub Actions, you can use concurrency to prevent overlapping runs in the same group. That's an execution mechanism, not a check that the business action hasn't happened yet.

It's important to read the queue behavior: a group's default allows one active run and one pending run, and a new pending run can replace the previous one. A setting that cancels an old run sometimes fits code testing, but can be wrong when every request needs handling. Even execution order is no guarantee of the order requests arrived.

### Test a duplicate event and a late reply too

The first experiment should include a reply on time, a reply after closure, the same reply twice, and a case where someone already performed the action. In each case, check the result in the system, not just the message the agent returned.

Success is one correct action, or a correct decision not to act, with state you can understand in hindsight. Merely receiving the reply is only a step along the way.
faq: What should you define before the agent starts waiting?
A source and identifier, a reply that allows continuing, the action boundaries, an end to the wait, and a last verified state.
Does concurrency prevent duplicate tickets?
It can prevent overlapping runs, but it doesn't prove a ticket wasn't created yet. You need to check the system before acting.
What do you do when a creation attempt ended in a timeout?
Check whether the result exists before retrying. No response is not proof the action failed.

human-review-ai-pull-request.title: How do you review a PR an AI agent wrote?
human-review-ai-pull-request.summary: Check that the change solves the right problem, ask for test evidence, and verify the change's boundaries. Automatic review is another feedback layer, and human approval stays a decision about the product and the system.
human-review-ai-pull-request.hook: In my post about team automations I described opening a PR, self review, and comment handling. I also gave credit to Ofir Cohen for a routine that expanded the process. That infrastructure prepares a change for review, but it doesn't replace the decision about what's right to bring into the system.
human-review-ai-pull-request.body:
**Short answer:** Check that the change solves the right problem, ask for test evidence, and verify the change's boundaries. Automatic review is another feedback layer, and human approval stays a decision about the product and the system.

### Start with the problem and the decision

Before reading a single line of code, ask for a short description: what changed, why it's needed, what stayed outside the task, and how the result was checked. Compare the description to the original request and the diff. A convincing explanation is not evidence the code does what was written.

Example: an agent was asked to fix handling of a missing file. If it also changed the output format, there's an extra product decision here that needs checking. The example isn't a client case, but a way to spot scope expansion.

### Demand a test that can fail

Ask for the commands that ran, their result, and what wasn't tested. A regression test should distinguish between the behavior before the fix and the behavior after it. A green result from tests that don't cover the fault isn't enough.

Also check error scenarios, permissions, and sensitive data when they're part of the change. A database change requires addressing migration and the way back. The level of testing should match the risk, not only the size of the diff.

### Use automatic review as additional feedback

GitHub's current documentation notes that Copilot code review can miss problems, and can also suggest an incorrect comment. The explicit recommendation is to verify the feedback and combine human review. So both code written by an agent and a fix suggested by a review tool need checking.

You can ask for early feedback on a draft-state PR, handle the relevant comments, and only then ask the team for review. Availability and settings depend on the plan and the account's permissions. You don't need to buy an extra tool to use this checklist.

### Re-check after a change

A review refers to a specific version of the code. In GitHub's documentation, Copilot doesn't necessarily check every push again unless configured to. After a significant fix, verify that the tests and the review cover the current version, and don't rely on an approval given before the change.

Branch protection rules can require checks and approvals before a merge, and dismiss approvals that went stale after a code change. That's an option for protecting the process, not a claim that every repository is set up this way.

### Finish with a decision you can explain

Before merging, check: does the result match the request, did the change stay within boundaries, is the evidence sufficient, and what risk remains. If information is missing, write what's missing instead of marking everything as checked.

An agent can shorten part of the preparation work. Whoever approves still needs to understand why the change should enter the system and what will happen if it fails.
faq: Does AI review replace human review?
GitHub recommends verifying Copilot's feedback and combining human review. An automatic tool can miss problems or suggest a wrong comment.
What should you ask an agent for before review?
A change description and scope, test commands and results, a regression test, and what wasn't tested. Compare the explanation to the diff and the request.
Do you need a new review after every fix?
Verify that the tests and the review cover the current version. A significant change can require re-testing and re-approval.
