native-tool-before-custom-agent.title: When should you pick an existing tool instead of building an AI agent?
native-tool-before-custom-agent.summary: Start from the outcome and the constraints, check whether an existing tool meets them, and build an agent only for the gap that remains. Compare the whole process, including maintenance, permissions, and failure handling, not just the first demo.
native-tool-before-custom-agent.hook: In my post about the wave of AI announcements I described an MCP tool for Jira that looked impressive, and then I found the plugin I already had was more convenient for my need. Since then this is a useful question before building: what's missing in the existing process, not which new tool can be added.
native-tool-before-custom-agent.body:
**Short answer:** Start from the outcome and the constraints, check whether an existing tool meets them, and build an agent only for the gap that remains. Compare the whole process, including maintenance, permissions, and failure handling, not just the first demo.

### Define the outcome before picking a tool

A request like "I need a bot to organize the tasks" already contains a solution. The outcome can be smaller: getting a clear list of open tasks with owners and dates. Sometimes a saved filter in the system that already exists is enough.

Write what needs to happen, who uses the result, where the data comes from, and which actions require approval. The distinction between reading and changing data matters even in a small process.

### Check the existing way on a real example

Example: a team wants an alert when a task is blocked. Before building an agent that searches conversations and updates tasks, you can check a blocking field and a built-in alert in the work management tool. If the system can't identify the reason from a conversation, that may be the gap where AI adds value.

The example is a suggested process, not a description of a client project. The check should use information you're allowed to share, and include a case with no change or no answer too.

### Compare the full process

An existing tool can save new code, but it also requires adaptation and permission checks. A custom agent can work across systems and understand free text, but you need to define what it does when the source is unavailable, when the reply is unclear, or when the action was already done.

Alongside the result, check human working time, errors, duplicates, ease of fixing, and ongoing cost. Don't present demo-building time as time saved in work. Also record separately the time the agent is only waiting.

### Build only the missing part

When an existing tool covers most of the way, you can keep the data and actions in it, and add an agent for one focused stage: summarizing a conversation, classifying a request, or suggesting the next step. That way you can test the addition without replacing the whole system.

In my public grok-bot-skills library, distill-need starts by identifying the need rather than sticking to the proposed solution. It's adapted from melech-distill-need by AdirD, with credit and license in the source. It's a useful framework for making a decision, not proof that every agent or every skill was tested in practice.

### Choose by evidence from the experiment

Continue with the option that delivers the outcome with clear boundaries and maintenance you can hold. If an existing tool is enough, that's a good engineering decision. If a clear gap remains, you can define a small agent task with a success check and a way back.
faq: How do you know if you really need an AI agent?
Define the outcome and check an existing tool on a real example. An agent is needed when a defined gap remains that the existing way doesn't cover.
What do you compare in a small experiment?
Check the result, human working time, errors, duplicates, permissions, maintenance, and ongoing cost. Waiting time is recorded separately.
Do you need to replace the existing system?
Sometimes it's enough to add an agent for a focused stage and keep the data and actions in the existing system.

keep-agent-context-current.title: How do you keep context files and Cursor rules up to date?
keep-agent-context-current.summary: Check claims against the current code, tie the check to a change that could age them, and distinguish a real fault from an example or a historical document. The agent reports only a gap it can explain and prove.
keep-agent-context-current.hook: In my post about context files I told how a check on a project found a description of six SDK packages when there were actually ten. Later, a scan surfaced 124 references that looked dead, and only four were a real problem. Those are numbers from that one case, not an error rate you can project onto other teams.
keep-agent-context-current.body:
**Short answer:** Check claims against the current code, tie the check to a change that could age them, and distinguish a real fault from an example or a historical document. The agent reports only a gap it can explain and prove.

A wrong rule attached to every task can mislead the agent again and again. A context file is part of the development process, so it needs maintenance too.

### Start with what's actually loaded

Pick claims you can verify: a package location, a test command, a service name, a path, or a component count. For each claim, look for a source in the code, a config file, or current documentation. If there's not enough source, mark "needs checking" instead of declaring the claim wrong.

### Check the rule type

Per Cursor's current documentation, project rules are kept in .mdc files under .cursor/rules. Fields like description, globs, and alwaysApply determine when the rule is attached. A rule with alwaysApply: true is included in every conversation, so a stale claim inside it gets wide distribution.

For a rule that applies to only part of the code you can set matching file patterns. For a simple instruction document you can use AGENTS.md. Check that the format and location fit your tool, not just that the file exists in the repo.

### Give the scan context

A path that doesn't exist is the start of a check, not a conclusion. It could be an example, output generated at runtime, content excluded from git, or a plan kept for history.

Check next to every finding: what the document tries to explain, whether the file was supposed to exist now, and whether the current change broke the reference. You can keep a historical document and mark it as such instead of rewriting it as if it describes the system today.

### Tie the update to the change

When a service is added, a folder structure changes, or a test command is replaced, check the instructions describing it in the same change. A review close to the changed code gets more context than a general scan months later.

The Cursor documentation recommends pointing to canonical examples instead of copying content that already exists in the code. A reference reduces duplication, but you still need to check that it's valid and that the example itself fits.

### Ask for a short report with evidence

An illustrative prompt:

"Check the context files related to this change. For every gap, show the sentence in the document and the current source that contradicts it. Distinguish an example, a historical document, and a fault. Propose a small fix only when there's evidence. If everything is fine, finish without unnecessary comments."

Silence isn't skipping the check. It's a valid result when the agent found no gap worth the team's attention.

### Check that the rule helps

After an update, try a small task the rule should apply to. Verify the agent uses the updated path, command, or instruction. Merely saving the file doesn't prove the tool loaded it or that the instruction improved the result.

Start with a few rules that recur in the work. Add a rule when a repeated mistake is found, and remove duplication already handled by code or a checking tool.
faq: When should you check that context files are current?
When a code change affects the structure, services, or work commands described in them, and in a periodic review of rules that always apply.
Is every reference to a missing file a fault?
No. Check whether it's an example, output generated at runtime, content excluded from git, or a historical document.
What's the difference between an .mdc file and AGENTS.md?
In Cursor, .mdc files under .cursor/rules include metadata for scope control. AGENTS.md is a simple alternative in Markdown format.

coding-agent-success-criteria.title: How do you define for a coding agent what counts as success?
coding-agent-success-criteria.summary: Attach to the task a result you can check, change boundaries, required tests, and who approves completion. The agent should return evidence from the run, alongside what wasn't checked.
coding-agent-success-criteria.hook: In my post about defining success for agents I distinguished between "do a refactor" and a task with a preserved interface, clear boundaries, and tests. The principle stays useful even for a small fix: the result should be defined before the agent declares it's done.
coding-agent-success-criteria.body:
**Short answer:** Attach to the task a result you can check, change boundaries, required tests, and who approves completion. The agent should return evidence from the run, alongside what wasn't checked.

When you ask to "fix the bug", the agent can pick a solution that looks reasonable but changes behavior nobody meant to change. A good definition narrows the choice before the code is written.

### Define behavior, not just a file to edit

Write what the user or the calling code should receive. For example, as an illustration: a file-reading function should return the same data after the fix. A missing or corrupt file should keep returning an error to the caller. Returning an empty dictionary instead of an error is not a fix of the same behavior.

### Give the test a chance to fail

Keep a case that shows the fault before the fix. The same test should pass after it. A test that passes on the original code too is not evidence this fault was fixed.

A public example from the DDD project illustrates the difference. A Python function passed tomllib.load a file opened in text mode. The experiment record documented a TypeError before the change. The fix was to open the file in binary mode, "rb", as the Python 3.11 documentation requires. After the fix two tests passed, and an additional test confirmed a corrupt TOML file still raises TOMLDecodeError. That's an experiment by the project's author, not mine and not a measure of time savings.

### Separate success from permissions

Write what may be changed and what stays outside the task: public interface, dependencies, secrets, other files, or deployment. You can allow a fix and running tests in a trial folder without allowing a global install or publishing.

An instruction file can remind the agent of the boundary. It doesn't replace access permissions, environment separation, or approval from whoever owns the system.

### Ask for a completion you can check

An illustrative template:

"Fix this fault without changing the public interface. Keep a test that fails on the original code and passes after the fix. Check the error behavior too. Edit only the permitted files, with no new dependency and no deployment. At the end show the change, the commands you ran, the actual results, and what remains untested."

In the completion report I want to distinguish four things: code written, a test run, an observed result, and approval for use. Those are different stages. You can complete the local fix and still wait for review or another environment check.

### Decide what happens when the test fails

Set upfront whether the agent may try another fix, should stop, or must return to a stable version. Also define when to turn to a human: missing information, a deviation from the permitted files, or a change touching real data.

That way the same task can move to another agent without losing its wanted result and boundaries.
faq: What's the difference between a task and a definition of success?
The task says what to do. The success definition says which behavior should result, how to check it, and what the boundaries are.
Does a passing test prove the whole system is fine?
It attests to the case and the environment that were checked. You need to state what wasn't tested and not infer the whole system from it.
Does an instruction file give the agent permission to publish?
No. Task instructions are no substitute for access permissions or approval to deploy or take an external action.

ai-adoption-small-business.title: How do you start adopting AI in a small business without developing anything?
ai-adoption-small-business.summary: Pick one problem that repeats every week, match it to an existing tool, measure for a month, and only then expand.
ai-adoption-small-business.hook: In a talk I gave at the "Lashevet" workspace in Shafayim, I spent 45 minutes on a live demo: I took ideas from the audience and turned them into websites. The lesson for a small business is to start with an experiment you can see and test, instead of buying several tools at once.
ai-adoption-small-business.body:
**Short answer:** Pick one problem that repeats every week, match an existing tool to it, measure for a month, and only then expand.

There are five steps.

**1. Choose one process.** Not "bring AI into the business", but something specific: answering inquiries, scheduling appointments, drafting price quotes, tracking leads.

**2. Measure what it looks like today.** How long does it take? How many inquiries get lost? Without an opening number you cannot know whether you improved.

**3. Look for an existing tool.** Almost every common problem already has a ready-made tool. Custom development is rarely needed in a small business.

**4. Start small.** One user, one case, two weeks. Check answers manually at first.

**5. Decide in advance when to stop.** If there is no improvement after a month, cancel the subscription. A tool that does not save time is not worth its price.

**Common mistake:** buying five tools at once. Every tool requires setup and maintenance.

vibe-code-project-rescue.title: The project built with Cursor, Lovable or Bolt doesn't work. What now?
vibe-code-project-rescue.summary: Stop asking the AI for more fixes, check logs, environment variables and the deployment, and narrow the problem down to one thing before fixing.
vibe-code-project-rescue.hook: In my experiment with Lovable I built The Useless Web in about an hour of copying, pasting and improving. In the post I wrote back then, I emphasized the gap between a fast prototype and code that fits production. That is exactly the reason to stop and check logs and structure when a project gets stuck, instead of just asking for another fix.
vibe-code-project-rescue.body:
**Short answer:** Stop asking the AI for more fixes, check logs, environment variables and the deployment, and narrow the problem down to one thing before fixing.

When a project created with AI gets stuck, the cause is usually one of these.

**1. An unread error.** Open the browser console and the server logs. The message usually says what is broken. Paste it in full, not as a free-text description.

**2. Environment variables.** The app works locally and breaks in deployment because API keys or URLs are missing in the runtime environment.

**3. Dependencies and updates.** A version that updated and broke something. Check what changed most recently.

**4. Lost context.** After many rounds of "fix it", the model adds code that contradicts existing code. Try going back to a stable point (the last working commit) and asking for one small change at a time.

**5. Architectural debt.** If everything is mixed into one file, every fix breaks something else. Here it is better to sort out the structure before continuing.

**When to get help?** If several hours have passed with no progress, or if the app has real users and data.

I diagnose stuck projects: a basic one-hour diagnosis for 450 ILS, followed by an estimate based on scope. The work is asynchronous and flexible. cursor-team-adoption.title: How do you roll out Cursor in a development team?
cursor-team-adoption.summary: Start with shared rules and a small pilot, not licenses for everyone. Then measure usage and cost.
cursor-team-adoption.hook: After we rolled out Cursor in the team, I noticed developers no longer wait for an answer to every code question. In my post I described how they ask the chat, understand, and move forward on their own. That is a change in the team's work habits, beyond buying licenses.
cursor-team-adoption.body:
**Short answer:** Start with shared rules and a small pilot, not licenses for everyone. Then measure usage and cost.

These are my lessons from leading the Cursor rollout at Elementor, in an engineering organization of 50+ engineers.

**1. Pilot before rollout.** A small group of volunteers, four to six weeks, and real tasks.

**2. Shared rules files.** Repo-level Cursor rules fix code style, conventions and common mistakes. Without them every developer gets different results.

**3. An internal community.** A forum or "guild" where developers share prompts, tricks and failures. Peer learning is faster than top-down training.

**4. Code review.** Code written by AI must go through human review. You can add an automated review that learns from the team's comments and stays updated with the rules.

**5. Measure usage and cost.** Without measurement, the costs surprise you. Track usage per developer, and check whether it translates into output.

**6. Security and privacy.** Define which repositories and secrets are not exposed to the tool.

**Common mistake:** assuming the tool alone will improve productivity. The process around it is what matters.

cursor-rules-from-code-review.title: How do you turn code review comments into rules Cursor can use?
cursor-rules-from-code-review.summary: Collect comments that repeated across several pull requests, check the team actually agrees on them, and then write short, focused rules inside the repo.
cursor-rules-from-code-review.hook: I asked my agent to build pr-rulebook from an idea that came up in conversation. In the post I published, I told both about the result and about the rule that was rejected in the experiment. The failure is what helps understand how to turn review comments into useful knowledge, without turning every comment into law.
cursor-rules-from-code-review.body:
**Short answer:** Collect comments that repeated across several pull requests, check the team actually agrees on them, and then write short, focused rules inside the repo.

A comment like "we already said you need to validate the input here" is a sign of team knowledge that never reached the place the agent reads. The goal is to move that knowledge into rules you can check and change.

**1. Collect evidence, not just phrasings.** Pick human comments from merged PRs. Check what changed following the comment. Repetition across several PRs is stronger evidence than two comments in the same discussion.

**2. Separate a convention from a momentary preference.** A recommendation that is right for one file may be wrong in the rest of the system. Next to each rule, keep a link to examples and to the original discussion, and someone from the team reviews it before use.

**3. Write a rule you can act on.** Instead of "write quality code", write what to check, when, and which file has a correct example. This is a suggested phrasing, not a client rule: "In new API routes, validate input before calling the database, following the pattern in the project's example file".

**4. Keep the rule in the right place.** Per Cursor's documentation, project rules are stored as `.mdc` files inside `.cursor/rules` and managed in Git. A rule can be applied by file type, by relevance, or manually. That way the whole team works against the same source, not against one developer's private prompt.

**5. Start small and test on real code.** Cursor recommends keeping rules focused, under 500 lines, and splitting topics. That is a guiding bound for a rule, not a target to fill. A short rule that prevents a repeating mistake beats a procedures book the agent struggles to apply.

In the documented pr-rulebook experiment, 15 PRs and 45 human review comments were scanned in the Ruff project. Two candidate rules were found, and only one passed testing. A good reminder: repetition in text is the start of a check, not an automatic approval to enforce a rule.

**When is this a fit?** When a team repeats the same comments over and over, and when it already uses Cursor or a coding agent. The rules help transfer context, but they do not replace tests and human review.

Do rules replace code review?

practical-ai-workshop-small-business.title: How do you choose an AI workshop for a small business that you leave with a deliverable?
practical-ai-workshop-small-business.summary: Choose a workshop built around a real business task, demand practice with a deliverable, and decide in advance who will keep using it after the workshop.
practical-ai-workshop-small-business.hook: In a talk I gave at the "Lashevet" workspace in Shafayim, I took ideas from the audience and built websites from them in real time. People watched their own idea become something they could open and test. From that experience I start the question about an AI workshop: what will the participants be able to do themselves at the end?
practical-ai-workshop-small-business.body:
**Short answer:** Choose a workshop built around a real business task, demand practice with a deliverable, and decide in advance who will keep using it after the workshop.

A goal like "get to know AI" is too broad to tell whether the workshop succeeded. A goal like "build a draft price quote based on our services" lets you check a result.

**What do you prepare beforehand?** One process, an example that contains no sensitive information, and a person from the business who knows the work. You can work with a dummy document or data stripped of identifying details. These are practice materials, not approval to upload private information to an external tool.

**What should happen during the workshop?** A short explanation, a demonstration, and then the participants do it themselves. The business owner should know how to fix the deliverable and understand what requires human review, not just watch a lecturer type.

**Which deliverable counts as success?** A template for a price quote, a draft answer to repeating questions, or a small process you can repeat. A demo website is a prototype; publishing a business website requires additional checks of content, forms, accessibility and security, depending on the use.

**How do you vet the instructor?** Ask for an example of an exercise and of the deliverable a participant builds. A lecture can fit exposure to ideas, and a workshop fits practice. Choose by the goal, not by the number of tools that appear in the slides.

In my Shafayim talk I split the time into 45 minutes of explanation and 45 minutes of live demo building websites from the audience's ideas. That is the format I described in the original post, not a rule every workshop must copy. My quote from there sums up the direction: "All that's left for you is to try."

**What do you do the week after?** Go back to the chosen task, use the deliverable, and write down what worked and what still needs fixing. If nobody opens the deliverable again, check whether the right task was chosen and whether instructions are missing.

The participants finish with a deliverable for a real task and know how to use it and check it again.

One task and a work example without sensitive information, together with a person who knows the process.

plan-before-coding-agent.title: What should you decide before starting to build with a coding agent?
plan-before-coding-agent.summary: Define who will use the product, where it will run, who will maintain it, and how it reaches users. Then choose a tool and ask the agent to build a small experiment that validates the choice.
plan-before-coding-agent.hook: In my post about consulting agents and coding agents, I told about a friend who started building in Claude Code and only near the end discovered the tool did not fit some of the requirements. From him came my principle: first figure out what you need to build and operate, then choose what to write the code with.
plan-before-coding-agent.body:
**Short answer:** Define who will use the product, where it will run, who will maintain it, and how it reaches users. Then choose a tool and ask the agent to build a small experiment that validates the choice.

A tool that produces a pretty screen still has to fit the product's life after the demo. When I plan the work, I separate the product decision from writing the code.

### Start from the user and the process
Write one action the user needs to complete. For example, a content editor needs to publish a page without opening a task for a developer. That is a test you can demo and check, not a general feature list.

### Check the way out
For an app: how do you distribute a version, who manages the store account, and how do you ship an update? For a content site: who edits the content, and how do you check the page is search-accessible? For a business system: where is the data, who is allowed to access it, and how do you recover from a failure? These are check questions. The answers depend on the product and the tool you choose.

### Write a short decision
You can use an ADR, an Architecture Decision Record. Martin Fowler describes it as a short document that records one decision, its context, and its consequences. Next to the choice, I suggest writing what the alternatives were and what would make us re-examine the decision.

A starter template:

- The problem the product solves and the first user.
- The constraints: distribution, permissions, maintenance and budget.
- Two alternatives worth checking.
- The choice and its reason.
- An experiment that proves the important action can be completed.
- Who owns it after the experiment works.

### Give the agent a bounded task
An example prompt, for illustration: "Before writing code, present two implementation approaches that fit these constraints. For each, state what we will need to operate and what is still unknown. Then propose a small experiment to test the main risk."

After deciding, ask for an implementation of the first action only. If the risk is deployment, the experiment must include deployment. If the risk is content editing, have a real editor test it. That way the choice rests on a working action, not on the impression from the first screen.
faq: What is the difference between a planning conversation and writing code?
The planning conversation clarifies requirements, constraints and alternatives. Writing the code implements a choice you can already test.
Do you need an ADR for every small change?
The document is useful for a significant decision with alternatives and consequences. A simple local change can stay in the task description.
What should the first experiment include?
The core action and the risk that needs validating, such as deployment or content editing by a user.

feature-to-marketing-with-ai.title: How do you translate a technical feature into an explanation for the marketing team with AI?
feature-to-marketing-with-ai.summary: Give the agent the feature's changes and documents, ask for an explanation of the problem and the value to the user, and then check with the feature owner what is actually available before using the text externally.
feature-to-marketing-with-ai.hook: I wrote on LinkedIn about a process we ran in the team: we connected Cloud Cursor to a Slack channel, and the content person asked it to explain a feature from the commits, the pull requests and the documents. The interesting work was translating the development material into the language of users.
feature-to-marketing-with-ai.body:
**Short answer:** Give the agent the feature's changes and documents, ask for an explanation of the problem and the value to the user, and then check with the feature owner what is actually available before using the text externally.

A developer thinks about implementation. A content person needs to explain who the feature helps and at what moment. The agent can prepare the draft that connects the two, as long as it gets the right source material.

### Prepare a source package
Pick the pull requests, the task description, the product documents and the tests related to the feature. State what is already merged and what is still open. If there is a usage limitation or a gradual rollout, attach that too. The distinction between planning and what is available right now matters especially in text that will reach customers.

### Ask for user value
An example prompt, for illustration:

"Analyze the attached changes and documents. Explain to a non-technical user what the feature does, which problem it solves, and when it is worth using. Separate available capabilities from work that is still open. For each major claim, state which source it rests on. If information is missing, mark it instead of filling it in yourself. Do not include code or infrastructure details in the user text."

### Check before publishing
Go over the draft with someone who knows the feature:

- Does the text describe the available version?
- Can the user perform the described action?
- Does the explanation leave out an important limitation?
- Is there a promised result that has no test behind it?

You can keep the source references in the internal document, and remove them from the customer version after the check. The goal is a clear explanation with a trail you can verify.

### Connect it to an existing process
At our place we used a dedicated Slack channel to start the work with Cursor. Per Cursor's current documentation, mentioning @cursor with a prompt can launch a Cloud Agent from inside Slack. The setup requires connecting a code provider, choosing a repository, a privacy check and billing settings. Check permissions and costs before connecting another team.

You can apply the same principle without Slack: prepare a source package, ask for a draft, check it, and hand it to the content team. The technical connection is chosen by the environment; the responsibility for correctness stays with the feature owner.
faq: What material should you give the agent?
Code changes, the task description, product documents and tests, with a clear distinction between merged work and open work.
Who approves the text for customers?
The feature owner checks availability, limitations and claims. The content team adapts the text to the audience after the check.
Do you have to connect Cursor to Slack?
You can prepare and check a draft without Slack. The connection is a way to start the work from inside the team's process.
